issue.title: WebMIDI: fix active pot panel title lookup
issue.body:
Fix the active pot panel lookup to use the element ID defined in index.html.

setActivePot() queried active-pot-name, while the corresponding title element is named active-pot-title. This caused a null element access when a pot or mix control attempted to display the active control panel.

issue.title: Don't lose a pot update that arrives while an effect is bypassed
Validate effect ids in the SysEx Set Routing Order command
issue.body:
Following up on the note in #22 that the "Allow re-ordering effects" reorg probably introduced other bugs. This is one in the same area.

The 0x08 Set Routing Order SysEx handler stores each payload byte into effect_chain[] before validating it. The eff_id < EFFECT_COUNT check only gates the ->target write, not the store, so:

- an out-of-range id (e.g. 200) goes straight into the chain, and the audio loop then indexes effects[200] out of bounds every sample;
- duplicate ids get past the append-unrouted loop below (which assumes the routed part is a distinct set), so a routing order like [3,3,3,...] pushes effect_chain_len up to 27 on a 15-byte array.

load_scene() already validates next_id > 0 && next_id < EFFECT_COUNT - 1 when walking the saved chain, so this just applies the same rule on the live-routing path and skips already-routed ids.

I can't build the firmware here (no Pico SDK on this box), so I modeled the routing-order builder plus the append loop and checked both cases: [200] makes the old code leave 200 in the chain (effects[] OOB), and [3]x14 drives effect_chain_len to 27; with the validation both stay bounded at 14.

issue.title: fix: give phaser a unique effect priority
issue.body:
klon.h and phaser.h both declared `// PRIORITY: 50`. gen_effects.py assigns each effect's ID from its index in a stable sort by priority, over files enumerated via `os.listdir()`. With a priority tie, ordering falls back to filesystem order ΓÇö which varies by machine/filesystem ΓÇö so klon and phaser could silently swap their MIDI/SysEx effect IDs between builds. The script's duplicate-ID guard doesn't catch this since post-sort IDs stay unique.

Fix

- Bump phaser to PRIORITY: 55 (unique; sits between klon=50 and flanger=60, leaving klon's ID unchanged).
- Wrap the effect enumeration in sorted(os.listdir(...)) so any future tie breaks deterministically instead of by filesystem order.

Verification

- No duplicate priorities across Software/effects/*.h.
- Ran gen_effects.py: exits clean, stable IDs (Klon=4, Phaser=5).

comment.body: This got fixed very differently today - I don't want priorities to have to be unique, but you are right that the sorting should be stable. So I just made the filename the second key in the sort.

issue.title: Move screen down and turn it around 180┬░?
issue.body:
Right now assembling these things is unnecessarily complicated due to the wiring of the stomp switches and the screen.

The stomp switches just need to have their own PCB and another FFC cable. Easy enough, except for the whole "need to move things around and do another board revision.

The screen is annoying because it comes with the 4-pin header already soldered, and I want a Qwiic connector. I could just do a simple dupont-to-qwiic thing, except the pin headers are also where the audio and power jacks are. So I have to desolder the pin header just to solder the qwiic wires to it. The end result is fine, but it's pointless extra work.

I could turn the screen around which would put the pin header much more centrally and I could just keep it. I'd have to lay out the main pedal board entirely, but that's not that big of a deal, and I need to do a board revision anyway to connect the stomp switches and LEDs differently.

The screen would be "upside down", but the sh1107 makes it easy to just scan it out in a reverse direction, so that's a minor setup issue.

More annoyingly, the PCB for the OLED screen isn't centered, and I'd have to move the visible part of the screen down a few mm and do new enclosures for that reason.  But I should do that anyway for the stomp switch movement, so...

As with the stomp switches, I'm not ready to really do this movement yet, and I'l just leaving a note for future Linus.

issue.title: Intelligent design
issue.body:
Commenting on your response to me about the purpose of all this:

```
It's not like the algorithms are new or particularly interesting. It's all just trying to learn basic DSP techniques - and for use in a pretty limited environment at that, so it's not even _fancy_ DSP techniques.
```

Looking at the way it is evolving now - I would not in any way equate 'fancy' with 'good', quite the opposite. Nothing is new under the sun - and to me, 'interesting' is both simple and practically useful in general. Since you're not making pedals on demand, it would be impossible to please everyone personally anyway. Unless that's what you intend to do :)

issue.title: Move foot switches further apart?
issue.body:
Ricky Sheaves points out that people who actually use guitar pedals rather than just design them for fun have big feet and prefer the stomp switches further apart.

These are 32mm apart (centered on the 125B enclosure at ┬▒16mm), and Ricky says that he uses ┬▒19.05mm which still fits the enclosure.

He also has them further down (at 44.45mm down from center) while mine are at 40mm down.

I picked round metric numbers that looked ok. And Ricky is clearly used to using Freedom Units (19.05mm is 3/4", and 44.45 is 1 3/4").

While I don't think I'm ready to embrace the insanity that is the US Customary System, I should probably just do ┬▒20mm apart and 45mm down.

... except I'd have to get new enclosures made. So for now I'm leaving this note for when I create a pcb for the stomp switches and LEDs, which I also need to do because I don't want to solder wires like some kind of animal.

issue.title: Bad flex design
issue.body:
Just a note to myself to rethink the flex board design. 

I didn't realize that the flex coverlay doesn't support the same capabilities as a normal solder mask, so the flex board rules for trace to pad separation are quite different from the ones I used. 

So the usb-stomp board may or may not actually work due to solder creeping under the coverlay and shorting to nearby copper. 

Live and learn.

issue.title: fix(usb): resolve thread safety in audio RX FIFO, stack memory dangling pointers, and non-blocking MIDI
issue.body:
Key Fixes:

1. Thread-Safe Audio RX Buffer (`tu_fifo_t`)
   - Replaced manual custom head/tail ring buffer indexing with TinyUSB's native thread-safe `tu_fifo_t`.
   - Prevents pointer tearing and race conditions between the core task loop (`usb_audio_task`) and hardware IRQ handlers during audio streaming.

2. Stack Memory Safety in Control Transfers
   - Allocated control transfer descriptors (`vol_range_resp`, `sample_freq_rng_resp`, and `conn_cluster_resp`) as `static` file-scoped variables inside `tud_audio_get_req_entity_cb`.
   - Previously, local stack pointers were passed to `tud_audio_buffer_and_schedule_control_xfer`, leading to potential memory corruption when transfers were processed asynchronously via DMA after function return.

3. Non-Blocking MIDI Packet Writes
   - Removed the blocking `while (!tud_midi_packet_write)` loop inside `usb_midi_write`.
   - Guarantees the CPU and main loop will not lock up or stall audio processing if the host unplugs or stops polling the MIDI endpoint.

4. Descriptor & String Cleanups
   - Replaced raw string descriptor mapping with a clean dynamic UTF-16 conversion helper (`tud_descriptor_string_cb`).
   - Aligned USB interface class and association descriptors for cleaner host enumeration.

Testing
- Verified USB Audio streaming and MIDI packet processing on RP2040 hardware.
- Confirmed host control transfers complete without memory access faults or dropped USB packets.

issue.title: parametric_eq: fix gain math, pot only delivered ~half the requested dB
issue.body:
_biquad_peaking / _biquad_loshelf / _biquad_hishelf (audio/biquad.h) take a gain argument and compute A = sqrtf(gain) internally ΓÇö i.e. they expect gain = A┬▓. Every other caller passes exactly that via db_to_level(db) = 10^(db/20): see klon.h:62, cabsim.h:70, frenchie.h:287.

parametric_eq.h is the lone exception. Its peq_pot_A(db) = 10^(db/40) is the correct RBJ value of A itself ΓÇö but it's passed in where the function wants A┬▓. So the internal sqrtf turns it into 10^(db/80), and a band dialed to +20 dB only produces about +10 dB. Both audio and OLED graph share peq_pot_A, so they agree with each other, but the response undershoots the pot labels ("LS Gain" LINEAR(-20.0 20.0) = 0.0 dB) and the graph's own axis (+20dB -> y=0).

Fix: drop peq_pot_A(), use db_to_level() like the other three effects.

I might be misreading intent here ΓÇö if thesofter-than-labeled range is deliberate, feel free to ignore. But it looked off against both the dB labels and every other biquad call site, so flagging it.

comment.body: Bah. This was not the first time a bad interface caused this confusion. Thanks.

issue.title: Require 4 bytes before reading the SysEx Set Parameter value
issue.body:
Small bounds fix in the new SysEx handling.

The Set Parameter command reads sysex_buf[0..3] (cmd, eff_id, pot_idx, val) but only checks sysex_len >= 3. sysex_len includes the command byte, so a valid message is 4 bytes long. A truncated 3-byte message (F0 7D 03 <eff> <pot> F7, no value) passes the check and val is read from sysex_buf[3], which this message never wrote. Since sysex_buf is static and not cleared between messages, that's the leftover value byte from a previous SysEx, so the pot gets set to a stale value instead of the message being ignored. Save Scene just below reads [0]/[1] and checks >= 2, so this is only lining Set Parameter up with that.

I couldn't build the firmware here (no Pico SDK on this machine), so I modeled the byte consumer and the guard in a small script to confirm the behaviour: after a valid write of value 123, a following truncated 3-byte Set Parameter reads 123 back out of buf[3] under >= 3, and is correctly rejected under >= 4.

issue.title: Move STATE_DUMP_CC below the pot CC allocation range
issue.body:
The generated MIDI CC map for the pots now reaches CC 127, and STATE_DUMP_CC (119) ended up inside that range. handle_midi_packet() matches STATE_DUMP_CC before the dense_midi_map[] lookup, so CC 119 - currently the Frenchie amp's "Level" pot - can't be controlled over MIDI; it does a state dump instead. Moving STATE_DUMP_CC down next to the other utility CCs fixes it without renumbering any pot.

Verified by regenerating effect_map.h/.js: dense_midi_map[119] is now a normal pot entry, CC 23 is unused by any pot, and the rest of the map is unchanged.

Unrelated things I noticed while here, not touched in this change: the pot allocation runs into 120..127, which MIDI reserves for Channel Mode messages, and two effects share PRIORITY 50 so their relative order (and CC numbers) depends on directory listing order.

comment.body:
I've manually merged the first commit in that series, since it was very obviously just me being incompetent.

The MIDI fixes I'm skipping not because they look wrong, but because I need to really rethink how the MIDI setup works. The current design is just too annoying for any real work, and it's more than just the index overlap. It's just a bad design. It really was a quick hack to test the concept - my very original external control mechanism was using a hacked-up HID protocol thing just so that I could test things by connecting it to my computer - which I do anyway just to upgrade the firmware.

The MIDI thing was me realizing that I should use proper standard interfaces both - and use real MIDI ports and not just the MIDI-over-USB thing. The whole project is more about me learning the hardware side, so the "real MIDI ports" part was interesting, and I now have Typa-A TRS MIDI jacks on my test pedal.

But the actual MIDI protocol details was something I didn't feel very strongly about, and it's literally just a quick AI-generated hack. And it's all just *wrong*.

I find the WebMIDI interface very useful for testing, but at the same time it has a few fundamental problems.

For example, the actual original real physical UI is in some ways superior. Particularly the 10-band EQ. I *cared* about that one, so it actually has a usable UI and shows a proper frequency response. In contrast, the WebUI is just showing a garbage visual representation and is not actually useful.

But the MIDI side *could* just make it all much more useful in a real situation, but it would involve much more than just making sure the numbers don't overlap. Right now, if you add an effect or even if you just add or remove a setting to an existing effect, all the MIDI CC numbers change. Which makes any MIDI pedal programming stale and useless. Even for the WebMIDI UI it's a horrible pain, because it means that you have to match the version of the WebUI exactly to the version that the pedal was programmed to. It's just *bad".

So right now the MIDI side is "showing that the concept can work", but it's not realistically useful.

I'd need to really think about it, and it probably needs other features too, like just having "scenes" that you can program so that you don't have to send 10+ MIDI messages - with random CC numbers that change if the firmware gets updated - to switch from one setting to another.

It's made worse by the fact that I still haven't even decided what I want the pedal to even look like. I like the super-compact pedal that I use for testing - it has literally just the stomp switch to turn the effect on/off, and you can only change the settings of it over MIDI (either USB or TRS Type-A) and it works. I have some stereo-capable hardware now, but I haven't had time to actually fix up the software side, so it's still just mono. But I don't think that minimal version is actually usable because the MIDI programming situation is so painful.

And even if I fixed that, I do think I'd want to have *some* control on the pedal itself, even if it's just a "switch between scenes" and/or something like master volume. For example, the noise gate actually seems to work really well, but even if that's the *only* thing you were to want to use the pedal for, having to connect it to a phone and the WebMIDI interface just to set the gating level if you move to a new place that is more/less electronically noisy seems like a horrible UI decision.

At the same time, I don't love the 128x128 screen I used. It's cumbersome to install, and it's simply not very pretty either. The best you can say about it is that it's very functional.

Oh well. Enough excuses.

Anyway, I have a handful of ugly prototypes. I've actually sent out pedals to a few people. But I only make one or two of each of my hardware designs, and some of the designs are better than others. So I could send you a pedal if you are an actual likely user of it and actually use MIDI on a guitar pedalboard, but..

(And while the designs are all open and in that Hardware/ directory, it's sadly not realistic for people to make their own pedals. It's *possible* to do: those kicad design files are complete and I'm not holding anything back.

But you have to have enough of a hw background to know how to get them manufactured and correct for the whole "need to fix up rotation and offsets of random components" when the kicad component origin or rotation doesn't match exactly with the manufacturing house origin and rotation. And it's not a cheap hobby: none of the components are very expensive per se, but when you manufacture just a handful of those things, all the one-time overheads add up, and the end result is that manufacturing costs are non-trivial.

So realistically, I can send out individual pedals, but I need to be *really* convinced it makes sense to do so.
